periods.analysis: Digital Service Adoption opened the series at 65.7%, above the >=60% target and solidly green, with no prior quarter or delta yet to compare. This is a good baseline for Council because it reflects the cleaned HarborConnect service catalog, not a one-time campaign spike. The strongest contributors were utility e-bill enrollment, online recreation registrations, and permit intake through the GovAccess front door for the 38 highest-volume services. Departments did the right operational work here: counter staff used the same service codes as the portal, which keeps the reporting cycle clean and makes the adoption story credible.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green result by keeping the monthly HarborConnect data-quality review on the first Tuesday after close, with department sign-off before the Council dashboard is refreshed. Extend the QR-code handoff at City Hall, the Marina office, and the North Harbor Library so residents who arrive in person can still complete eligible transactions digitally. Ask each department to nominate one additional high-volume form for digital conversion before the 2024-Q4 reporting deadline.

periods.analysis: Digital Service Adoption held at 65.7%, a 0.0 point quarter-over-quarter movement from 65.7%, and remained green against the >=60% target. Flat is acceptable this quarter because holiday counter traffic, year-end business tax questions, and walk-in recreation refunds usually pull the mix back toward in-person service. The HarborConnect team still protected the baseline by suppressing duplicate CRM tickets and reconciling 1,142 utility account lookups that previously inflated assisted-service counts. For Council, the key message is consistency: adoption did not slip while departments were closing books and staffing holiday schedules.
periods.recommendations: Sustain performance by keeping the Q4 duplicate-ticket rule in the ClearPoint source file and documenting it in the metric notes before the next packet. Extend adoption by adding a one-page “finish this online” script for cashiers handling business license renewals and utility starts. Have IT and Finance review the top 10 in-person payment reasons by January 15 so the next push is based on actual resident friction, not guesswork.

periods.analysis: Digital Service Adoption increased to 67.8%, up 2.1 points from 65.7%, keeping the measure green and moving the trend in the right direction. The lift tracks with the January mobile permit renewal release and the “Two Minutes Online” resident nudge placed in utility bills and library Wi-Fi landing pages. Planning also helped by routing simple roof, fence, and water-heater permits through the PRM-204 workflow instead of email attachments. This is the kind of cross-department gain we want to show Council: small process fixes, clean data, and no drama at quarter close.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the gain by making the PRM-204 permit workflow the default for all eligible minor permits and auditing exceptions weekly through March close. Extend the campaign to Public Works service requests by adding HarborConnect links to crew door tags for missed carts, potholes, and streetlight reports. Keep the adoption dashboard refreshed by the fifth business day so departments can see their own contribution before the Council version is finalized.

periods.analysis: Digital Service Adoption reached 69.6%, up 1.8 points from 67.8%, and remains green with a healthy cushion above the >=60% target. The quarter benefited from summer camp registration, beach parking permit renewals, and inspection scheduling moving through the same authenticated resident profile. Parks staff at the Seabreeze and East Harbor counters used assisted-digital tablets rather than paper waitlists, which preserved access while still counting the transaction in the digital channel. The arc is encouraging: two consecutive increases tell Council this is becoming normal operating practice, not just a portal launch effect.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green trajectory by keeping assisted-digital tablets staffed during peak Parks and permitting windows, especially the 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. rush. Extend the authenticated profile model to special event applications before the August coastal festival season, starting with the 25 repeat applicants from last year. Ask departments to flag any paper-only exceptions by service code so we can separate policy barriers from simple form-conversion work.

periods.analysis: Digital Service Adoption edged up to 69.8%, a 0.2 point increase from 69.6%, and stayed green. The smaller movement is not a concern by itself; at nearly 70%, the easy conversions are mostly behind us and the remaining transactions are more complicated. Coastal event permits, back-to-school recreation changes, and new-resident utility starts all created mixed-channel activity where staff often had to verify documents in person. The good news for Council is that Harborview held the gain through peak summer demand while maintaining clean service-code mapping in the dashboard.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the current level by continuing same-day digital completion support at City Hall for residents who bring documents but can finish the application online. Extend adoption by building a document-upload checklist for coastal event permit applicants and sending it 14 days before their renewal window. Watch the new-resident utility-start cohort specifically, and have Customer Service test a pre-move email sequence before the next quarter closes.

periods.analysis: Digital Service Adoption declined to 67.7%, down 2.1 points from 69.8%, but it remains green and still above the >=60% target. I am marking this as a friendly watch item, not an alarm, because the drop aligns with year-end walk-in payments, senior recreation renewals, and several paper-heavy business license corrections. The data review found that the BL-118 license correction path and REC-77 scholarship adjustment were the largest non-digital clusters, not a broad loss of resident confidence in HarborConnect. For Council, the honest story is that we stayed green, but the plateau has turned into a manageable dip that needs owner-level follow-through.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green status by protecting the proven digital pathways for utilities, permits, and standard recreation registration while we fix the exceptions. Extend adoption by converting BL-118 and REC-77 into guided online forms with Finance and Parks acceptance testing completed before February month-end. Add a weekly exception report for any service code with more than 100 in-person transactions so the next decline is visible before quarter close.

periods.analysis: Digital Service Adoption rebounded to 71.2%, up 3.5 points from 67.7%, putting the measure back on a stronger green trajectory. This is the clearest proof point in the series that the Q4 dip was operational and fixable, not structural. The guided BL-118 license correction form, Parks scholarship upload, and lobby QR coaching at three counters all went live before the March reporting cutoff. Departments deserve credit here: they closed the loop quickly, and the dashboard now shows a higher adoption level than any prior quarter in this sequence.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the rebound by keeping the weekly exception report active for one more quarter, even though the status is green, so we do not lose the discipline that produced the fix. Extend the guided-form pattern to residential encroachment permits and short-term rental renewals, starting with the 60-day renewal cohort. Before the Council update, capture two department examples in the notes field so the result reads as service improvement, not just a percentage.

periods.analysis: Digital Service Adoption increased again to 71.6%, up 0.4 points from 71.2%, and remains green with an 11.6 point margin over the >=60% target. The smaller gain is expected after the Q1 rebound; we are now operating in the harder stage where each additional point requires targeted redesign. The remaining paper concentration is mainly in business renewals needing documentation review, residential encroachment permits, and a small group of recurring marina lease amendments. For Council, the chronological arc is strong: Harborview moved from a 65.7% green baseline to 71.6% while improving data quality and keeping departments aligned to the reporting calendar.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the 71.6% result by locking the current service-code definitions and requiring department validation by the third business day after quarter close. Extend adoption by piloting appointment-to-digital conversion for marina lease amendments and encroachment permits, with tablets and document scanning available at the first contact. Set a practical next internal milestone of 73% and assign owners for the three remaining paper-heavy cohorts before the next Council strategy check-in.

periods.analysis: Digital adoption rose from 47.9% to 50.3%, but remains 4.7 percentage points below the September target of 55%. Online permitting went live in September; that milestone does not by itself establish that residents have switched channels.
periods.recommendations: Review transactions by service type and focus assisted digital conversion on the remaining paper-heavy workflows.
